content: 1. Primary amoebic meningoencephalitis (PAM) is typically contracted when contaminated water enters the nasal passages. This is most commonly associated with recreational water activities, such as swimming in pools, spas, or natural surface waters heated by the sun, as well as industrial cooling waters and geothermal springs. However, in some cases, no direct link to recreational water exposure is identified. 2. The incidence of PAM is highest during the hot summer months, when water temperatures are favorable for the growth of the causative organism and recreational water use is more frequent. Transmission through ingestion of contaminated water or food, or via person-to-person contact, has not been reported. 3. Naegleria fowleri, the organism responsible for PAM, has been detected in drinking water supplies. Although unproven, it is possible that organisms derived from drinking water, such as those introduced into swimming pools, may play a role in transmission. Water supplies that seasonally exceed 30°C or consistently exceed 25°C can support the growth of N. fowleri. Periodic monitoring of such water systems is recommended. 4. Maintaining a residual disinfectant concentration of at least 5 mg/L in water distribution systems has been shown to control N. fowleri, provided the disinfectant remains effective throughout the system. Additional measures, such as reducing biofilm organisms, can limit the availability of nutrients and inhibit the growth of N. fowleri. 5. Due to the environmental nature of N. fowleri, traditional microbial indicators like E. coli or thermotolerant coliforms are not reliable for detecting its presence in drinking water supplies. 6. Toxoplasma gondii is a coccidian parasite for which cats serve as the definitive host. Infected felines harbor the parasite in their intestinal tract, where sexual reproduction occurs. In humans, the actively multiplying asexual form, known as tachyzoites, is an obligate intracellular parasite. Over time, tachyzoites transform into bradyzoites, which replicate slowly and form tissue cysts. 7. In the natural cycle, rodents containing infectious cysts are consumed by cats, where the cyst wall is digested, and bradyzoites invade the intestinal epithelial cells. This leads to the development of oocysts, which are excreted in feline feces. These oocysts require 1–5 days to sporulate in the environment and can infect susceptible hosts. 8. Human toxoplasmosis is usually asymptomatic, but in some cases, flu-like symptoms, lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly may occur 5–23 days after ingestion of cysts or oocysts. Dormant cysts in organ tissues can reactivate in immunosuppressed individuals, leading to severe neurological disorders or pneumonia, which can be fatal. 9. Congenital toxoplasmosis is often asymptomatic but can result in chorioretinitis, cerebral calcifications, hydrocephalus, thrombocytopenia, and seizures. Primary infection during early pregnancy may lead to spontaneous abortion, stillbirth, or fetal abnormalities. 10. Toxoplasmosis is globally prevalent, with 15–30% of lamb and pork meat estimated to be infected in many regions. By the third decade of life, approximately 50% of the European population is infected, with rates as high as 80% in France. Oocysts from infected cat feces can contaminate water sources, but practical methods for detecting T. gondii oocysts in water are limited. 11. Humans can become infected with T. gondii by ingesting oocysts from contaminated soil or water, or by consuming undercooked or raw meat containing tissue cysts. Transplacental transmission also occurs. Outbreaks of toxoplasmosis have been linked to contaminated water sources, such as creek water in Panama and a drinking-water reservoir in Canada. 12. Drinking water contaminated with T. gondii oocysts has been identified as a source of outbreaks. While oocysts are larger than Cryptosporidium oocysts and can be removed by filtration, little is known about their response to water treatment processes. Preventing contamination of source water by wild and domestic cats is a key control measure. 13. Helminths, or parasitic worms, include nematodes (roundworms) and platyhelminths (flatworms, such as trematodes and cestodes). While most helminths are not transmitted through drinking water, exceptions include Dracunculus medinensis (Guinea worm) and Fasciola spp. (liver flukes). 14. Dracunculus medinensis is the only nematode significantly transmitted via drinking water. The eradication of Guinea worm disease has been a global health goal, with significant reductions in cases achieved through interventions such as safe water provision and health education. 15. Guinea worm larvae are released into water when the female worm emerges from a blister or ulcer on the host's skin. The larvae are ingested by Cyclops species (water fleas), which serve as intermediate hosts. Humans become infected by consuming water containing infected Cyclops. 16. Symptoms of dracunculiasis include allergic reactions such as urticaria, erythema, and pruritus, followed by the emergence of the worm. In 50% of cases, the worm is fully extruded, and the lesion heals. However, complications such as secondary infections and abscess formation can occur, leading to prolonged disability. 17. Fascioliasis, caused by Fasciola hepatica and Fasciola gigantica, is primarily a foodborne disease but may also be transmitted through drinking water in hyperendemic regions. The life cycle involves intermediate hosts, such as snails, and the release of infectious metacercariae into water. 18. Control measures for waterborne helminths include filtration of drinking water to remove Cyclops, chlorination to inactivate intermediate hosts, and the provision of safe water sources such as boreholes and protected wells.
